To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) NRC equations for predicting N excretion in feces and urine of lactating cows were confirmed and extended by the current study; 2) NRC equations can be used with confidence to estimate N excretion in the urine and feces of lactating dairy cows; 3) N excretion in both urine and feces can be predicted from DM intake and dietary N intake; and 4) NRC equations are not improved with inclusion of milk production or body weight.

The amount and composition of N excreted in manure can be accurately predicted from dietary DM intake and N consumption; the amount of feces excreted is 6.1 kg (34.3% DM intake), with 88.2 percent of feces volatile solids; and urine is 0.9 percent of DM intake, with 47.8 percent of urine volatile solids.

N excretion in feces and urine is highly predictable from DM intake, that feces and urine contain similar amounts of most nutrients, and that the amounts of nutrients in feces and in urine vary in a predictable manner with DM intake.
In summary, our research is concerned with
determining the effects of dietary protein level and source on the amount and composition of manure from lactating dairy cattle.
the development of a model to predict N and other nutrient excretion in feces and urine of lactating cows.
developing equations to predict N excretions and other manure characteristics for use in manure N budgets.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the amount and proportion of N excreted in manure are determined primarily by the amount of dietary DM consumed and the amount of N consumed.
the NRC equations are adequate and that the equations presented in this paper are unnecessary.

the NRC (2001) equations are adequate for predicting N excretion of lactating dairy cows fed diets with a wide range of protein concentrations and sources, and that NRC (2005) equations for estimating N excretion in feces and urine of beef cows can be used for predicting N excretions in feces and in urine for lactating dairy cows.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
dietary protein effects on N utilization by lactating cows are primarily due to effects on N intake, and that the effects are relatively small and can be accounted for by simple equations.
dietary protein level and source have little effect on N excretion of lactating cows.
dietary CP level and source are of little consequence in determining the amount of N excreted by dairy cows.
The main takeaway from our work is that
manure N flow from cows can be predicted accurately from DM intake (or milk yield) and CP intake.
the amount of manure excreted daily is very closely correlated with DMI and can be estimated from it.
N excretion by dairy cows is very closely related to DMI, and that N excretion is not closely related to either milk yield or BW.
